content.title: Gary Woodland gets first PGA Tour win since 2019 U.S. Open, weeks after revealing PTSD diagnosis
content.text: Gary Woodland thought he might have lost the ability to live a normal life, let alone play professional golf. Now he is a PGA Tour winner again.Woodland, 41, won the Texas Children’s Open on Sunday, weeks after he publicly revealed his ongoing battle with PTSD, which stemmed from a 2023 brain surgery. As Woodland walked up the 18th fairway at Memorial Park in Houston, the crowd erupted into an ovation, and Woodland’s playing partners, Nicolai Højgaard and Min Woo Lee, stopped to clap for him. After he tapped in his final putt of the week, he looked up, took a massive sigh of relief, and then broke down in tears.“We play an individual sport out here, but I wasn’t alone today,” Woodland said. “Anybody that’s struggling with something, I hope they see me and don’t give up.”Woodland earned his fifth PGA Tour win Sunday, and the victory means he will qualify for the 2026 Masters. He failed to earn an invitation last year, missing the first major championship of the season for the first time since 2016. He shot 21 under par for the tournament in Houston, winning by five shots over Højgaard.Your browser does not support the video tag.The timing of the win is especially significant for the 2019 U.S. Open champion. It was only at this month’s Players Championship that Woodland decided to open up about a personal struggle that has not only impacted his game, but also his quality of life. And it stems from a traumatic battle with his brain health.Woodland had brain surgery in September 2023 to remove a tumor that was causing him extreme anxiety and panic attacks. In the months leading to the procedure, Woodland did not understand what was wrong with him — he’d wake up in the middle of the night, clutching his bed, thinking he was falling to his death. And the symptoms came out of nowhere. “I thought everything was going to kill me,” Woodland said at the time.Doctors eventually discovered that the noncancerous lesion was pressing against the part of the brain that dictates fear. Woodland’s episodes were diagnosed as partial seizures. The 2023 craniotomy was successful, but the tumor had to be removed through a “baseball-sized hole” in Woodland’s skull.When he miraculously returned to golf four months later, Woodland’s body was healthy, but he continued to experience mental symptoms such as hypervigilance and panic. Woodland described an instance at the Procore Championship last year, in which a volunteer accidentally startled him in the middle of a tournament. He broke down on the spot, and his vision remained blurry for the rest of the round. Woodland finished the event with the help of his close friend and caddie, Brennan Little, and finished T19.“I don’t know how I did it,” Woodland told The Athletic at the Players. “I couldn’t see, so he told me where to hit it — every putt.”One year ago, he was officially diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder. But Woodland kept the state of his mental health private while he continued to play professional golf and while the golf community celebrated his return to the course. Woodland has understandably struggled to put the pieces together in his game while silently working on himself. This year, he had made three cuts on the PGA Tour in seven starts before Houston. His best finish had come last week at the Valspar Championship, a T14.“The start of this year, those four weeks I played, I was in a dark place,” Woodland said. “Luckily, I had a week or two off there and kind of reset a little bit. Then I decided to come out with (the diagnosis) and kind of got some confidence last week.”That was the week after Woodland decided to open up about his ongoing battle for the first time. He took it upon himself to reach out to Golf Channel and ask for a sit-down interview, hoping it would help take a weight off his shoulders. Woodland said he felt he was expending unnecessary energy hiding his PTSD diagnosis, and his inner circle of medical consultants encouraged him to do anything that would help relieve stress. The plan worked.“I literally feel like I got a thousand pounds off my back that day,” Woodland said Thursday. “It was hard to do. I was crying going into the interview, and I left feeling a thousand pounds lighter.”After Woodland took the important step forward of sharing his story, he was able to channel more of his focus into his swing and his equipment. Working with coach Randy Smith — who also works with world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler — Woodland decided to switch to his old, stiffer iron shafts. He also started swinging harder. For several seasons, while fighting his health, Woodland began losing speed, but now he’s back to full power. He ranked No. 7 in driving distance in Houston, with an average of 321 yards off the tee.“(Smith) wanted me to get back to swinging hard and aggressive, kind of playing to my strengths,” Woodland said earlier this week. “It’s been a process to get there, but we’re starting to swing at it again like I used to. Definitely comes with some confidence.”That confidence — and a new sense of relief — helped Woodland post rounds of 64, 63, 65 and 67 to step back into the winner’s circle again. His game is rounding into form just in time for the major season, but that does not mean Woodland is healed forever.In his post-round news conference, Woodland revealed that on the back nine of Friday’s round he “got extremely hypervigilant” when a few individuals got too close to him inside the ropes. Woodland leaned on his private security but could not calm down for the remainder of the round.“I got into scoring, I bawled my eyes out, I reset and was able to come back out and take care of stuff after,” he said.Woodland explained that opening up about his diagnosis helped him seek proper support with the PGA Tour, including heightened security. The added resources have been vital to his resurgence in form these past two tournaments.“Today was a good day, but I’m going to keep fighting,” he said. “I’ve got a big fight ahead of me, and I’m going to keep going. But I’m proud of myself right now.”
